answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
Additionality: as a Renewable Energy Certificate (REC) supplier, we are beginning to hear from prospective corporate customers that in anticipation of the upcoming Greenhouse Gas Protocol Scope 2 changes, they will begin requiring the procurement of RECs that can demonstrate “additionality”. When I request their definition of “additionality”, the prospective customer clarifies that by “additionality”, they mean a project that is not yet operational and will represent a new source of renewable electricity on the grid. I have heard this definition from many prospective customers that purport plans to continue following Greenhouse Gas Protocol guidance. At this definition’s level of simplicity, RECs purchased under these customers’ definition of “additionality” would not pass any of the tests described in Section 7 of the Consequential Electricity-Sector Emissions Impacts Consultation document. Therefore, it seems that aligning corporate procurement practices with Greenhouse Gas Protocol guidance is already proving to be a challenge.

Alternative Impact of Electricity Project Incentives: our company works closely with Native American tribes, which are often located in rural areas that make renewable energy development infeasible due to supply chain limitations. I am familiar with dozens of renewable energy projects owned and operated by tribes. None would have been built without philanthropic support from government or nonprofit sources. Based on my experience and that of my colleagues, I can confidently state that tribal renewable energy projects cannot be built without philanthropic support. While philanthropic capital is the sole factor enabling project development, this does not mean that the incentives generated by the project, such as RECs, cannot be impactful once the project is operational. REC revenue can provide real monetary benefits to tribal project owners over the operational life of the project; for example, eliminating the need to raise grant funding for unexpected operations, maintenance, and decommissioning costs if REC revenues are held in a fund dedicated to those activities. These costs are typically not feasible to fund in advance of project construction due to strict government and foundation grant application requirements. It does not appear that the full scope of impact that incentives such as RECs are considered in the consequential accounting methodology. Even if they cannot demonstrate additionality in a new renewable energy project being constructed, it is still possible to demonstrate additionality in a project’s continued operation. My company sees this as an unintended consequence of the structure of this methodology.

answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why secondary effects should be excluded
answers.text: Secondary effects are small enough in many cases that they may be excluded.

answers.label: Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text: In line with our response to Question 18, there is value in evaluating emissions impacts on the grid annually, as the actual impacts will differ from what is modeled at the outset of the project. This can give incentives value in keeping projects online during unexpected operational failures during the life of the project.

Requiredness of the common practice test
Why selected tests should be included
answers.text:
Regulatory: legally required interventions should not meet a definition of additionality
Barrier test: requiring a demonstration that the incentive helped the project overcome barriers is a flexible way to ensure that the incentive has value.
Positive list: this could allow for projects that don't fit a capitalist model of development and operation to ensure that the incentive it generates has value.
